translations.text: Discourse of our holy and blessed father Basil on fasting, chapter 1.
"Blow the trumpet at the new moon, at the head of the month, on the feast day of your rest": this is the command of the prophet.
But to us, more loftily than any trumpet and more powerfully than any musical instrument, Scripture announces in advance the feast of these coming days.
For we have learned the grace of fasts from Isaiah the prophet,
who cast aside the form of the Jewish fast and showed us the true fast, for he says:
"Do not fast for judgment and strife, but loosen every bond of wickedness." And again, the Lord says:
"Do not be sorrowful, but wash your face." Now therefore let us be just as we have been taught.
Let us not become sorrowful on account of these coming days, but let us be radiant toward them, as befits the saints,
for no one becomes crowned through negligence, and no one puts on the crown of victory and its adornment through sorrow.
Do not become sorrowful when you are being healed, for it is evil not to rejoice over the health of the soul,
but instead to grieve over the lack of food, and to have greater joy over the filling of the belly than over the care and brightening of the soul.
For satiety bestows its benefit on the belly, but fasting purifies and brightens the soul.
Rejoice, for a medicine that destroys sin has been given to you by the good physician. For just as worms
that have settled in the bodies of children are killed by a strong medicine, so too sin that has settled in the depth of the soul
is destroyed by fasting when it enters the soul, if only the fast is truly worthy to be called a fast.
For this reason the Lord says: "Anoint your head and wash your face."
Let this word be addressed to you as a mystery: whoever anoints himself is reckoned as one anointed; whoever washes himself is purified.
But understand the names of these bodily members spiritually, as referring to the inner man:
wash your soul from sins, anoint your head with the ointment of holiness, so that you may become a partaker with Christ, and in this way come to the fast.
Let your face not be sad like those of the hypocrites, for the face becomes sad at that time
when the mind of the inner man darkens the outer man with that perverse appearance and covers him with falsehood.
And the hypocrite is the one who puts on a foreign appearance before the assembly of people.
When someone is a slave, he will often change into the appearance of a master, and a poor man into the appearance of a king; so too in this world, as in a theater,
many alter their way of life as a show for people, when they have one thing in their heart and appear to people in a different guise.
Therefore do not change your appearance; such as you are, so appear to people.
Do not change your face to gloom in order to be thought a faster, and so that glory may deceive you.
For there is no profit in almsgiving done before people, nor in fasting that is done openly, for every good work
that is done as a show for people, the reward of such a work is not kept for the age to come, but is paid out here and now in the praise of people.
Approach, then, the gift of fasting radiantly, for fasting is a gift from the beginning, one that never grows old or ages, but is always renewed and flourishes.
Do you perhaps think that I speak of its antiquity as dating from the Law?
Fasting is older even than the Law [?]. Wait a little and you will find the truth of my word:
Do not think that the day commanded to Israel in the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month, was the beginning of fasting.
Come, then, and search out its antiquity, for it is not something newly discovered, but is a treasure of the fathers.
Everything ancient is honorable; feel reverent shame before the old age of fasting.
Fasting was given to us in Paradise, for Adam received this as the first commandment: "Of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat."
And this saying is the commandment of fasting. If Eve had then fasted from that tree, we would now have no need of this fasting, for:
"Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick." But since we have become weak through sin, let us now be healed through repentance.
But repentance does not come about without fasting, for when Adam transgressed the commandment, that decree was given to him which says:
"Cursed be the ground; thorns and thistles shall it bring forth for you."
Understand, then, O man, that hardship has been decreed for you and not delight; through fasting make God gentle toward you.
For that way of life in Paradise is itself an image of fasting, not only because man then lived among the angels and was like them through that want of food,
but also because all that human contrivance later discovered, the dwellers of Paradise knew nothing of at all.
Among them there was no drinking of wine, no eating of meat, nor anything else that disturbs and troubles human nature.
Because we did not fast, for that reason we were cast out of Paradise.
Now, then, let us fast, so that we may return there again. Do you not see Lazarus, how he entered Paradise through fasting?
Do not imitate that disobedience of Eve; do not again accept as counselor the serpent, who would counsel you to pity the flesh and urge you to eat.
Do not plead as an excuse the weakness and feebleness of the body, for it is not to me that you offer those excuses, but to him who knows all things.
Tell me, are you unable to fast? Yet are you able to gorge yourself and ruin your body with that weight of foods? And how can this be?
For physicians do not tell the sick to eat many kinds of food, but rather urge them to fasting and want of food.
And how can this be? You who are able to gorge yourself and bear that weight of foods, do you say, "I am unable to fast"?
What is easier and lighter for the body: to pass the night lightly on simple food, or to lie down weighed down by a multitude of dishes?
And not even to lie, but to toss and turn constantly, when the belly is bursting from the multitude of dishes and is in pain?
Or will you perhaps say this too, that a ship weighed down with cargo is more easily saved from the waves than one fitted out with a light load?
For even a small rising of the waves sinks the one weighed down by the great amount of cargo,
but the one that carries a load according to its own measure moves easily over the waves, for nothing hinders it.
In the same way a person's body, constantly weighed down by satiety, easily falls into illnesses, but the one that takes light and measured food
drives off even the sickness that is coming, as if it were rising waves, and from whatever infirmity it has, it is quickly set free as well.
Or does eating much benefit the weak more than eating sparingly?
Then sitting must be heavier than running, as you say, and rest heavier than fighting [?].
For the power of our nature quickly digests simple and measured food and turns it to a person's benefit,
but when it takes in a multitude and variety of dishes and then cannot overcome them, it brings various diseases upon the person because of this.
But let us turn back again to our first subject, so that we may speak of the antiquity of fasting, and how all the saints,
as an inheritance and a preserved patrimony, thus received and kept it.
For each father handed it down to his son, and therefore all received it, one after another, until this treasure came down to us as well.
There was no wine in Paradise, nor any eating of meat. After the Flood wine came to be; after the Flood God commanded:
"Eat everything, like the green plants of the field." Once the hope of perfection had been cut off, then God permitted enjoyment.
And the example of inexperience with wine is Noah, who did not know the use of wine, for people were not accustomed to drinking it.
And for this reason, since he had neither seen anyone else do it nor had experience himself, he fell into the passion of wine.
For Noah planted a vineyard and drank of its fruit and became drunk, not because he was a drunkard and disorderly, but because he was inexperienced in the measure of drinking it.
So recently discovered is the drinking of wine, and so ancient is the honor of fasting. For Moses too approached the mountain through fasting.
For if he had not been armed with fasting, how would he have dared to enter the cloud on the mountain from which smoke was rising?
Through fasting he brought down the commandment of God, written by the finger of God on tablets, and on the mountain fasting became the leader of the giving of the law.
But gluttony turned the people over to idolatry, for it is written: "The people [?] sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to sing.
The forty days' supplication and fasting of the servant of God were made useless by a single excess [?], for the divinely written tablets,
which fasting had brought, drunkenness shattered, for the lawgiver did not consider it fitting that a drunken people should receive the law of God:
In the blink of an eye the people, whom God had taught by those great gifts, fell into idolatry through the gluttony of the Egyptians. Set these two side by side and see
how fasting brings a person to God and how luxury becomes the betrayer of life.
Consider what it was that defiled Esau and made him the slave of his brother.
Was it not a single dish, for which he gave away his birthright? And was it not fasting together with prayer that granted Samuel to his mother?
Or who made mighty Samson invincible? Was it not fasting, through which he was conceived in his mother's womb?
Fasting gave birth to him, fasting raised him, fasting made him strong and brave, as the angel commanded his mother, saying:
"Let her eat nothing that comes from the vine, and let her drink neither wine nor mead."
Fasting gives birth to prophets and strengthens the mighty; fasting makes lawgivers wise.
Fasting is a good guardian of the soul and a wall for the body, an unerring and strong weapon for warriors and a tester of those who contend in struggle.
It drives away temptations, it is the anointing oil of the fear of God, the procurer of vigilance, the attester of purity.
In battles it shows itself victorious, in peace and tranquility it teaches stillness, it makes monks holy,
and it perfects priests in purity for the priesthood, for without fasting it is impossible to assemble for the priesthood, not only now,
in this true service of the mystery, but it was also given in the service of the old law, which was a type of this one.
This made Elijah a witness of that great wonder, for by a fast of forty days he purified his soul and so became worthy to see the Lord on Horeb,
as far as it is possible for a human being to see him. By fasting he gave that woman back her child, and through fasting he became victor over death.
And again, the voice that came from the mouth of that faster shut the heavens against that lawless people for three years and six months,
for he chose affliction even for himself, in order to bend the unbending heart of those stiff-necked people.
For this reason he said: "As the Lord lives, there shall be no water on the earth except by my mouth."
And through the famine he brought a fast upon all the people, which he did out of divine zeal, in order to do away with the wickedness born of luxury and ease.
And see what kind of life Elisha led. How did he stay with that Shunammite woman?
Or how did he himself receive the prophets? Was it not with wild herbs and a little flour that he fed them?
When they ate even the herb called tolype, those who had taken it would nearly have died, had that deadly poison not been removed by the prayer of the faster.
And so you will find that fasting has led all the saints to the divine life.
There is a kind of wood called amiante, which is not burned by fire, for as long as it is in the fire
it is like a glowing coal, but when it is taken out of the fire, it appears all the brighter, as if washed with water.
Such were the bodies of the three youths in the fire of Babylon.
And because of fasting they remained untouched, for in that great furnace of fire, like gold,
so they were unharmed by that fire, and they were even stronger than gold, for the fire did not melt them but kept them untouched within that flame,
which no one could withstand, which was kindled with naphtha and pitch and vine cuttings, and which rose as high as forty-nine cubits and burned up everything around it,
so that it killed many Chaldeans. And into such a fire they entered, and through fasting those youths trampled it down.
A breeze of wind with dew was given to them within that fierce fire, for the fire did not dare to touch even their hair, because their hair had grown through fasting.
But Daniel, that man of desires, who for three weeks ate no bread and drank no water, and who taught even the lions to fast, when he entered that pit:
for as with a stone, or bronze, or some other resistant material, so those lions were unable to bring their teeth near him.
Thus, as tempering tempers iron, fasting tempered that man's body and made it untouchable by the lions, for they did not open their mouths against that holy man.
Fasting quenched the power of fire and stopped the mouths of lions. Fasting raises prayer up to heaven and becomes its wings for ascending to God.
Fasting is the guide to rest, the mother of health, the teacher of the young, the ornament of the old, the good companion of travelers, the unerring housemate of those who stay at home.
A husband is not suspicious when he sees his wife fasting, nor again is his wife consumed with jealousy when she sees her husband fasting.
Where has anyone impoverished his house through fasting? Count your treasures today and count them afterward, and you will see
that nothing will be lacking from your house because of fasting. Because of fasting no animal laments its death;
nowhere is there blood, nor does the command issued by that tyrant, the belly, appear anywhere; the knife of the cooks is at rest.
The Sabbath was given to the Jews for rest, and it says: "So that your beast of burden and your servant may rest."
Let fasting be a rest from their continual labors for the slaves and servants and those who strive unceasingly to serve the belly.
Give rest to your cook, give leisure to your table servant, stay the hand of your wine pourer, and let him also cease who prepares those many kinds of [?] foods.
Let your house also grow quiet from its many tumults, and from the smoke and steam and the sizzling of frying pans, and from those running up and down who serve the belly as an evil master.
Even tax collectors sometimes grant a little rest to the people under their authority.
Let the belly also give some small rest to its servants; let it make an offering to us in these few days, the belly which always demands and is never satisfied;
which receives today and forgets tomorrow. When it is full, it speaks about fasting and praises it; when it is empty, those words are forgotten.

Fasting does not know the nature of debt. The table of one who fasts does not reek of interest. The inherited usuries of his father do not trouble the orphaned son of one who fasts, like snakes coiled around him.
And again, fasting is also a cause of joy, for just as a drink of water tastes sweet to the thirsty, so all food seems pleasant and sweet to the hungry.
For when fasting places itself in between and cuts off the heaviness of those many delicacies and of luxury, it makes you eager to eat.
And therefore, if you wish your table to be sweet and desirable, take upon yourself the labor of fasting.
But you are so mastered by great luxury that you destroy your own enjoyment without realizing it, and through your immoderate love of flavor you make the flavor of foods vanish and you ruin it.

For there is nothing so desirable that it does not become despised when one is constantly sated with it; but in the case of a thing that is not constantly acquired, being filled with it is something to be desired.
For this reason our Creator also ordained that our life should change from one state to another, so that in this way we may be grateful for the good things given to us.
Do you not see that the sun too is brighter after night, and wakefulness is sweeter [?] after sleep, and health is more longed for after the afflictions of sickness?
In the same way, eating is more desirable after fasting, both for the rich who have fine tables and for the poor who have nothing.
Fear the example of that rich man, for it was the delights of this life that handed him over to the fire; for it was not for injustice,
but for his luxury and soft living that he was condemned and tormented in the flame of the furnace. Now therefore water is needed, so that we may quench that fire.
And fasting is not needed only for the age to come, but it is also better for the body as well,
for great luxury leads the way to pains and collapses, when nature is thrown into turmoil and cannot bear the weight of the body's fatness.
See and beware, lest now you refuse to take water and in the end your heart longs for a single drop, like that rich man.
No one has ever become drunk from drinking water. No one's head has ached from water. No one who drinks water has needed another person's feet to walk,
nor have anyone's feet been bound up because of water, nor have anyone's hands become useless because of water.
For those who live in luxury cannot even manage to digest, and for this reason they bring excessive sickness on their bodies; but the complexion of one who fasts is beautiful.
He is not shamelessly flushed red, but is adorned with that beautiful and pure paleness; his eyes are held [?],
his steps are calm, and he has the appearance of prudence. He is not defiled by insolent laughter, he knows the measure of speech, and he has purity of heart.
Remember those saints of past ages, of whom this world was not even worthy,
who "went about in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, afflicted, ill-treated"; imitate their way of life.
If you wish to have a share with them as well. What gave Lazarus rest in the bosom of Abraham? Was it not fasting?
Likewise, the life of the great John was nothing but fasting; he had neither bed nor table,
Neither land to be plowed, nor oxen to bear the plow, nor wheat, nor baker, nor anything else belonging to this life.
Therefore, among those born of women no one greater than John the Baptist has arisen; and again, of the blessed Paul:
Among those other hardships, fasting too was his boast, and for this reason he was caught up to the third heaven [?].
And above all this, the Lord himself also fortified with fasting the flesh that he put on for our sake, and in this way took upon himself the attacks of the devil all at once,
to teach us that we should train and discipline ourselves by fasting, and through it take courage in temptations.
And again, through hunger he let the adversary come near, as if to lay hands on him, for he could not otherwise be looked upon by him, because of the height of his divinity,
had he not been brought low by that want to the level of human nature.
But when he was going up to heaven he took food, in order to make credible the nature of the risen body.
But you do not cease fattening and thickening your flesh, while your mind,
which you waste away through hunger for the life-giving and divine teachings, you do not care for at all.
Or do you not know that, as in a battle, the brave endurance of one combatant brings about the crushing defeat of the other and victory over him?
In the same way, whoever adds to the onset [?] of the flesh undoes the soul, and again, whoever orders himself toward the soul enslaves the flesh, for these are opposed to one another.
Therefore, if you wish your mind to be strong, tame your flesh with fasting, for this is what the Apostle says:
"The more our outer man wastes away, the more the inner is renewed," and again he says:
"When I am weak, then I am strong." Will you not disregard these perishable foods?
Will you not long for that unfailing table of the kingdom of heaven, which fasting prepares for you here beforehand?
Do you not know that by that immoderate satiety you fatten all the more the tormenting worm against yourself?
For who has ever, anywhere, received any share of divine grace through pleasure and luxury?
Moses, when he was receiving the second law, had recourse to a second fast as well; and the Ninevites, if even their beasts had not been made to take part in the fast,
would surely not have escaped that wrath of destruction. Or whose bones fell in the wilderness? Was it not those who craved meat?
As long as the manna and the water flowing from the rock were enough for them, they were overcoming the Egyptians, they were walking across the sea,
and there was no one feeble among their tribes. But once they remembered the meat of those cooking pots and turned back to Egypt in their desire, they no longer saw the land of promise.
Are you not afraid of this example? Do you not tremble at gluttony, lest it cast you too out of those eternal good things?
For neither would the wise Daniel have seen those visions, had he not made his soul radiant by fasting,
for heavy foods give off vapors like mist and, like a thick cloud, they muddy the radiances that come into the mind from the Holy Spirit.
And if the angels too have any food, it is bread, as the prophet says: "Man ate the bread of angels"; it is not meat.
Nor is it wine, nor those other kinds of dishes devised by the slaves of the belly. Fasting is a weapon for battle against the demons,
for "this kind is driven out by nothing else but by prayer and fasting."
Such, then, are the good things of fasting; but satiety and gluttony are the beginning of outrage and defilement,
for every kind of defilement immediately joins itself to luxury and drunkenness and the various forms of love of taste.
Of the bestial kind. Because of this, men became lustful horses, on account of the arousal and frenzy [?] that enters the soul from indulgence.
From drunkards come the perversions of nature, for they seek womanhood in men and manhood in women.
But fasting knows the measure even of marriage, and it chastens excess even in what the law permits, and by mutual agreement it grants leisure, so that they may persevere in prayer.
Do not limit the goodness of fasting to abstinence from foods alone, for true fasting is estrangement from evil things.
"Loose every bond of unrighteousness"; forgive your neighbor your anger; forgive him his debts.
"Do not fast for judgment and strife." You do not eat meat, but you devour your brother; you abstain from wine, but you cannot refrain from insult;
you hold out until evening without tasting anything, but you spend the day in the law courts. Woe to those who are drunk without wine.
Anger is a drunkenness of the soul, for it makes the soul senseless and rabid, just as wine does; and sorrow, again, is a drunkenness, for it too submerges the mind;
fear, again, is another drunkenness, when it arises where it ought not; for it says: "From fear of the enemy deliver my soul."
And so every passion that darkens the mind may rightly be called drunkenness.
Consider, then, an angry man: how he is made drunk by that passion, is not master of himself, is ignorant of himself and ignorant of those near him,
like someone fighting at night, he strikes at everyone, blunders against everyone, speaks without considering, and is hard to restrain.
He reviles, strikes, threatens, swears, shouts, bursts with rage, and fumes [?].
Flee from this drunkenness, and do not take on that of wine either; do not anticipate the drinking of water by drinking much wine; do not let drunkenness be your counselor toward fasting,
for there is no entering into fasting through drunkenness, just as there is no entering into righteousness through greed, nor into purity through defilement; and, to say it all at once:
there is no entering into virtue through wickedness. The door that leads to fasting is a different one, for drunkenness leads to defilement, but contentment in want leads to fasting.
The soldier first tests and exercises himself, and the one who fasts practices fasting beforehand.
Do not lay up beforehand a five days' drunkenness, as if taking revenge for those days and as if deceiving the lawgiver,
for you toil in vain: you weigh down the body and yet give no consolation to the want.
That treasure is not to be trusted which you pour into a pierced vessel, for the wine leaks out and goes its own way, and nothing else will remain to you from it but sin alone.
A slave flees from a master who beats him, yet you stay by wine, which is forever striking you on the head.
The good measure for the use of wine is the need of the body. But if you go beyond the limits, tomorrow you will come with a heavy head,
yawning, dizzy, and reeking of that rotten wine; everything will seem to go round about you, everything will seem to you a ruin.
Drunkenness brings on sleep, the brother of death, and then a wakefulness that resembles dreams.
Do you know whom you expect to receive within yourself? The one who said: "I and the Father will come and make our dwelling with him."
Why then do you first admit drunkenness, and shut the door against the Master so that he cannot enter into you?
Why do you urge the enemy to be first to seize your strong walls? Drunkenness does not receive the Lord; drunkenness drives away the Holy Spirit.
For as smoke drives away bees, so drunkenness drives away spiritual gifts.
But fasting is the beauty of a city, the calm of its streets, the peace of its households, the safekeeping of its possessions. Do you wish to see its honor?
Consider this evening and tomorrow's, and you will see the city changed from turmoil and uproar to calm.
But I pray that this present day may be like tomorrow in calm, and that tomorrow may fall short of today in nothing in brightness.
And may the Lord, who has brought us to this turning of the year, grant us that, like contestants,
we may show firmness and strength of endurance in these contests, and that we may reach that crowned day, that lord of days, which now is the remembrance of the life-giving passion,
and in the age to come is the recompense of our deeds, the just judgment of his Christ; for to him belongs glory, now and always and for ever and ever. Amen.
